title: Wedge Pop
teaches: The Wedge Pop as we trade it: a stock that corrected under its short averages rests a few tight days under them, then trades through the base's high and closes back above them on more volume. We buy at market through the pivot, no more than 4% past it, above the 200-day, with the stop a few cents under the pop day's low; a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

walkthroughs.title: TGT, March 2021: the clearest coil
steps: TGT, March 2021. A 17% correction with 15 of 15 closes under the 20 EMA, still above the 200-day.
A 10-day base, 166.83 to 181.79. The bars shrink to 0.44, the tightest of our ten. The pivot is 181.79.
2021-03-19: it trades through on 2.2x the base's volume. Buy at market, 181.80. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 179.58.
Failure mode: a fade back under the pivot, stop taken next day. Instead 3R comes the next session. Trim a third.

walkthroughs.title: RCL, July 2009: the gap through the pivot
steps: RCL, July 2009, early in a new cycle. A 34% decline, 14 of 15 closes under the 20 EMA.
A 4-day base, 11.80 to 12.95: the shortest the rule allows, right at the 200-day. The pivot is 12.95.
2009-07-15: it gaps open above the pivot, under the 4% chase line. Buy the open, 13.18. Stop under the day's low, 12.97.
Failure mode: a fade back into the base. Instead 3R comes the next session: a third off, stop to breakeven.

walkthroughs.title: STLD, March 2026: light volume, slow start
steps: STLD, March 2026. A 22% decline, all 15 closes under the 20 EMA. Then a 7-day base, 162.16 to 175.51.
2026-03-31: it trades through 175.51 on only 1.2 times the base's volume. A B-grade pop: normal size.
Buy at market, 175.52. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 171.31: 2.4% away, inside about 3%.
Failure mode: a fade back into the base. Instead 3R takes six sessions. Thirds at 3R and 5R, then 175 to 280.

questions.q: In one line, what is a Wedge Pop?
choices: A pop from a base under the EMAs
A bounce off a crash low
A pole that doubles in weeks
A gap down through the averages
questions.answer: A pop from a base under the EMAs
questions.why: A pop out of a tight base under the averages. It is the first point where a stock rallies back through its moving averages after a Reversal Extension. Deepvue says the same.
questions.lesson_line: A stock rests under its averages, the bars get small, then it pops back through them.

wrong.A bounce off a crash low: A bounce is not the setup. The pop comes after the stock rests under its short averages and then clears them.
wrong.A pole that doubles in weeks: That is the high tight flag's pole. The pop starts a new up-cycle after a decline.
wrong.A gap down through the averages: That is the mirror, a drop. The pop goes up through the averages.

questions.q: On a Wedge Pop the stop goes a few cents under the pop day's low.
questions.why: True. A few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. Kell did the same on CAVA: a stop set under the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the pop day's low.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.why: 4%. No buy more than 4% past the pivot. A pop day that runs further is a chase.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent past the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.sentence: No buy more than ___% past the pivot.

questions.q: Which pair of averages does Kell's cycle of price revolve around?
questions.why: The 10 and 20-day EMAs. They guide the intermediate trend in Kell's cycle. He keeps the 50 and 200-day simple averages for the longer trend.
questions.lesson_line: Kell's cycle lives on two short exponential averages. The slow lines are for the bigger trend.

wrong.The 50 and 200-day SMAs: Kell uses those for the longer trend, not for the cycle itself.
wrong.The 100-day SMA alone: No Kell page builds the cycle on one slow line. His cycle uses two short averages.
wrong.The weekly 40-week line: That is a weekly trend line from other methods, not Kell's daily cycle.

questions.q: A close back above the averages is enough to call a Wedge Pop.
questions.why: False. Many traders mistakenly believe the Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages. A cross alone is not a pop: it needs the tight base and the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: A cross is not a pop. First the tight base, then the trade through its high.

questions.q: On a Wedge Pop, what is the pivot?
choices: The highest high of the base
questions.answer: The highest high of the base
questions.why: The highest high of the base, the short-term resistance. Kell: the pivot forms as price swings between the lows and the averages.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the base's high before the open. That is the line it must trade through.

wrong.The Reversal Extension's low: That low marks the bottom. The pivot is the top of the base that forms after it.
wrong.The 200-day moving average: The 200-day is a line the stock must be above. It is not the buy point.
wrong.The pop day's close: The close comes after the buy. The pivot is set before the pop day.

questions.q: We buy a Wedge Pop with a market order as it trades through the pivot, in regular hours.
questions.why: True. A market order when it trades through the pivot, regular hours only. Entries are market orders.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the pivot. When it trades through, buy at market.

questions.q: Once the pop works, we add more shares at each new range.
questions.why: False. The full size at one price with one stop; no adding. Kell adds as each new range breaks. We do not.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one stop. The size goes on once.

questions.q: In Kell's words, what does a Wedge Pop signal?
choices: A bottom, and a new uptrend
A top, and a new downtrend
questions.answer: A bottom, and a new uptrend
questions.why: A bottom, and a new uptrend. It signals that a stock has bottomed and is starting a new uptrend. Kell's QQQ pop confirmed the low that way.
questions.lesson_line: The pop is the market telling you the low is in. Then you have a line to risk against.

wrong.A top, and a new downtrend: That is the Wedge Drop, the mirror. The pop starts an up-cycle.
wrong.A pause inside a downtrend: A pause under falling averages is the base. The pop is the break out of it.
wrong.A gap that must fill: Kell says the powerful pops often start with gaps. Nothing says they must fill.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.why: 3. The base needs at least 3 sessions after the low, at least half the closes at or under the higher average. Kell: price needs a few days to retreat.
questions.lesson_line: No base, no pop. A few quiet days under the averages come first.
questions.sentence: The base needs at least ___ sessions after the low.

questions.q: Volume drying up through the base raises the grade.
questions.why: True. Volume drying up through the base is the A+ cue. Kell's failed QQQ pops came with consistent distribution volume instead.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume in the base, loud volume on the pop. That is the picture.

questions.q: A pop day gaps up over the pivot. How does Kell read a gap there?
choices: Most strong pops start with gaps
A gap means it is too late now
Gaps fill, so wait for the fill
A gap does not matter either way
questions.answer: Most strong pops start with gaps
questions.why: Most strong pops start with gaps. Kell: most Wedge Pops that lead to new, powerful trends start with gaps. In our scan a gap open of 1% or more did better, not worse.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the averages is strength, not a reason to wait.

wrong.A gap means it is too late now: Not if it is still inside the chase line. Kell says the strongest pops often start this way.
wrong.Gaps fill, so wait for the fill: Waiting for a fill is a guess. Kell reads the gap as strength.
wrong.A gap does not matter either way: It matters: a gap up through the pivot is the A+ pop on our card.

questions.q: The first pullback into the rising averages after the pop is a separate setup, the EMA Crossback.
questions.why: True. The first pullback after the pop is the EMA Crossback, a separate setup and a new trade, not an add. Kell names the two in that order.
questions.lesson_line: Pop first, crossback second. Two setups, two trades.

questions.q: After the pop, which close says the pop failed?
choices: A close under the pop day's low
Any red day in the week after
A close under the day's open
questions.answer: A close under the pop day's low
questions.why: A close under the pop day's low. That means the pop failed, and the stop sits just under it anyway. If it fails, cut losses quickly.
questions.lesson_line: The pop day's low is the line. Under it, the pop is done.

wrong.A close under the 200-day line: Not the line. The pop is judged against its own low first, long before the 200-day.
wrong.Any red day in the week after: A red day can hold above the pop day's low. Noise is not a failure.
wrong.A close under the day's open: A red candle is not a failure by itself. The line is the pop day's low.

questions.q: A $12 stock that trades $15 million a day passes our liquidity rule.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. $15 million is short of it.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars and twenty million a day, or it is not on the list.

questions.q: The last 5 sessions averaged a 2.10 range; the 10 before averaged 3.00. What is the ratio?
questions.why: 0.7. The last 5 sessions' range over the 10 before. Our card wants under 0.85, so this base is tightening.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the shrink. Do not eyeball it.

questions.q: The pop day ran 100.00 to 106.00 and closed at 104.00. Where did it close, in percent of its range from the low?
questions.why: 66.7%. The close minus the low, over the day's range. Our card wants a close in the top 40% of the range, so this one passes.
questions.lesson_line: Where the pop closes grades it. Near the high is what you want.

questions.q: Bought at 175.52 with the stop at 171.31. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 188.15. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. The first third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: After the first third comes off at 3R, what is our next step?
questions.why: Another third at 5R, then trail the last third. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, the rest on the trail.

wrong.Sell the rest at 4R: No rule sells everything at 4R. The second third comes off at 5R and the last one trails.
wrong.Add back the third: No adds. The size goes on once, at one price.
wrong.Hold the rest to 10R: No fixed 10R target. The last third rides the trail.

questions.q: By our default, the stop moves to breakeven as soon as the trade is up 1R.
questions.why: False. Breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. The hard rule for that trim is a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: First third off, stop to breakeven. Then a stop-out costs about nothing.

questions.q: How do we trail the last third on a fast mover?
choices: A touch of the pop day's low
questions.why: A close under the 10-day. The 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers ride the 10-day. Steady ones get the 21-day.

wrong.A close under the 200-day: That gives back the whole move. The trail is the short average.
wrong.A fixed 8% under the high: Our trail is an average, not a fixed percent.
wrong.A touch of the pop day's low: That is near the first stop, long left behind by the time the last third trails.

questions.q: A pop still under 1R is given 20 trading days before it is sold.
questions.why: False. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. In our scan the median winner reached 3R in 3 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Good pops move fast. Ten days and nothing, the money goes elsewhere.

questions.q: Buy now, or wait?
choices: Wait for a tight day or pullback
Buy now, it is strong and moving
Buy half size now to be in
Buy now, stop at the pivot
questions.answer: Wait for a tight day or pullback
questions.why: Wait. 31.70 is more than 4% past 30.24. A pop day that runs further is a chase; wait for the first tight day or pullback after it.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss the pop than chase it. The tight day after it is the next door.

wrong.Buy now, it is strong and moving: Strong and too far away are both true. The line is 4% past the pivot.
wrong.Buy half size now to be in: Half of a chase is still a chase.
wrong.Buy now, stop at the pivot: Moving the stop to fit a late fill is the mistake. Chasing costs size; the stop stays under the day's low.

questions.story: The pivot is 30.24. You missed the first move. At 11:00 the stock trades 31.70 after one wide bar.

questions.q: Your fill would be 55.40. The 10-day average is 50.00. How far above it, in percent?
questions.why: 10.8%. More than 10% above the 10-day: too stretched to buy. Skip it.
questions.lesson_line: Read the stretch in percent before you buy. Past 10% over the 10-day, I pass.

questions.q: Fill 24.58, stop 23.68. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.66%. Wider than about 3%: a smaller position or a pass, never a tighter stop. That was CROX's stop in 2007, the widest of our ten.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Account 200,000. Risk 0.25%. Fill 181.80, stop 179.58. How many shares?
questions.why: 225. Account times risk percent, divided by the fill minus the stop, rounded down. The stop sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Buy?
questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. MU in March 2022 was this picture: the next day's low of 78.60 went through the 79.21 stop.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the chart. A report inside three days and I wait.

wrong.Yes, the picture is textbook: The picture was textbook on MU too. The report decides the next morning, not the chart.
wrong.Yes, at half size: Half size does not stop a gap through the stop. The rule is no new buy.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: A wider stop cannot catch an overnight gap, and the stop never gets wider to fit.

questions.story: A textbook pop after a 31% decline: through the pivot on 1.8 times the 50-day volume, closing at the high. The company reports tonight.

questions.q: Buy the open, or wait for a pullback?
questions.why: Buy the open. If it opens above the pivot, buy at the open when the gap is no more than 4% above it. 51.20 is inside that line.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the pivot inside the chase line is the A+ pop. Buy it.

wrong.Wait for a pullback to 50.00: Inside the chase line the open is the buy. Waiting for a dip can mean no trade at all.
wrong.Pass, gaps tend to fill: Kell says the powerful pops often start with gaps. A gap up is strength.
wrong.A limit order at 50.00: Entries are market orders. A limit under the market waits for a dip that may not come.

questions.story: The base's high, the pivot, is 50.00. On the pop day the stock opens at 51.20, above both averages.

questions.q: It gaps over the pivot and you buy the open. Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Exactly at the day's low price
8% under the fill, a wide stop
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. On a gap the day's low can sit above the pivot: RCL in 2009 did.
questions.lesson_line: The stop follows the day's low, wherever the gap puts it.

wrong.Exactly at the day's low price: A few cents under it, not on it. A stop on the exact low gets tagged by noise.
wrong.Under the 200-day moving average: That is a line the stock must be above, often far below. It is not the stop.
wrong.8% under the fill, a wide stop: A stop that far away is B- at best. The stop is the day's low.

questions.q: The stock trades 1,500,000 shares a day on average. Our ceiling on the position?
choices: No ceiling with a tight stop
questions.why: 15,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.150,000 shares: That is a tenth of the day's volume. You could not get out without moving it.
wrong.1,500 shares: That is a tenth of the line. The ceiling is 1%.
wrong.No ceiling with a tight stop: A tight stop cannot catch a gap. The ceiling stands.

questions.q: Wedge Pop or EMA Crossback?
questions.why: An EMA Crossback. A wedge pop comes after a correction spent mostly under the averages. A crossback is the first pullback into averages the stock already rides. DECK in May 2024 was a near-miss of this kind: a pullback inside an uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: Ask where the stock came from. Up from under the averages is a pop; down into them is a crossback.

wrong.Wedge Pop: A pop is the push up through the averages from under them. This stock has been riding above them.
wrong.A flat base breakout: A flat base is weeks in a box under a flat top. This is a dip to a rising line.

questions.story: A May 2024 chart. Fourteen sessions ago the stock popped back over its averages. Every close since held above the 20 EMA. Today it dips to the average and holds.

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop?
choices: No, a cross with no base or pivot
Yes, if the volume is heavy
questions.answer: No, a cross with no base or pivot
questions.why: No. A cross of the averages alone is not a Wedge Pop: it needs the tight base and the pivot. Kell: focus on price bars and volume.
questions.lesson_line: No tight base, no pivot, no pop. A cross is just a cross.

wrong.Yes, it reclaimed both averages: Reclaiming the averages is one part. Without the tight base there is no pivot to trade through.
wrong.Yes, if the volume is heavy: Volume grades a real pop. It cannot make a pop out of a ragged range.

questions.story: Price closed over both averages today. The two weeks before were wide and ragged, with no clear high to trade through.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the base looks clean
Take it, but only at half size
questions.why: Pass. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, and the Wedge Pop is not a parabolic long. AMZN in January 2019 was this case: it worked, best 7.46R, without us.
questions.lesson_line: A pop that works is not always our pop. Under the 200-day, I pass.

wrong.Take it, the base looks clean: A clean base under the 200-day is still under the 200-day. That rule is hard.
wrong.Take it, but only at half size: A hard rule has no half size. Under the 200-day there is no long.

questions.story: A January 2019 chart. A 36% decline, a 6-day base, and a pop on 1.1x the base's volume. The pop day closed 7.3% under the 200-day.

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop by our card?
questions.why: No. A pop on volume no higher than the base days is a cross of the averages with no demand. Kell's failed QQQ pops came with no increase in accumulation.
questions.lesson_line: The pop must bring buyers. Light volume through the averages is not a pop.

wrong.Yes, it closed above both: The close was right and the buyers were missing. Volume no higher than the base days ends it.
wrong.Yes, the base was tight: A tight base is half the setup. The pop day still needs more volume than the base.

questions.story: An 18% decline, then a 6-day tight base. It trades through the pivot and closes above both averages, on 0.88x the base days' volume.

questions.q: Two pop days: one closes near its high, one closes back under the pivot. Which grades higher?
questions.why: The close near the high. In our scan a close back under the pivot on the pop day cut the success rate to 23.1% against 46.5%, the strongest single cut.
questions.lesson_line: Where the pop day closes tells you if the pop is real.

wrong.The close under the pivot: That is the failure mode starting. A close back under the pivot was the strongest single cut in our scan.
wrong.They grade the same: The close grades the pop. Our card wants it above the pivot, near the high.

questions.q: A close back under both averages and inside the base, within 5 sessions of the pop, invalidates it.
questions.why: True. A close back under both averages and back inside the base within 5 sessions ends it. That is the failure mode: the pop fades.
questions.lesson_line: A real pop holds its ground. Back in the base means the pop is gone.

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.why: No. The index still making lower lows with its averages falling is an invalidation on our card. Kell avoided long swings until the index capitulated or gave a buy signal.
questions.lesson_line: A pop against a falling market is swimming upstream. Let the index turn first.

wrong.Yes, the stock is strong: Strength in one stock does not stop a falling market from dragging it down.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: A tighter stop than the rule only gets tagged sooner. The issue is the market, not the stop.

questions.story: Your stock pops cleanly through its pivot. The index is still making lower lows, its averages pointing down.

questions.q: What changes?
choices: Move the stop to the pivot
questions.why: The size, not the stop. If the honest stop is wider than about 3%, take a smaller position or skip; never tighten the stop to fit.
questions.lesson_line: Never shrink the stop to fit the size. Shrink the size to fit the stop.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3%: A stop pulled in to fit the size sits inside the day's noise. The stop never gets tighter to fit.
wrong.Nothing, size as normal: A wider stop at normal size is more risk. The size comes from the stop.
wrong.Move the stop to the pivot: The stop is the day's low. Moving it to fit is the mistake.

questions.story: Fill 50.00. The pop day's low is 48.20, so the stop sits at 48.15, 3.7% away.

questions.q: Same base, two pop days: one on 1.2 times the base days' volume, one on 2.5 times with a gap up. Which grades higher?
questions.why: The gap up on 2.5 times. The A+ pop gaps up through the averages and the pivot on clearly more volume than the base days. STLD popped on 1.2 times and still worked: volume grades.
questions.lesson_line: More volume and a gap grade the pop up. Light volume grades it down.

wrong.The pop on 1.2 times: Lighter volume is the weaker pop. It can still work, but it grades lower.
wrong.They grade the same: Volume and a gap are how the pop is graded. These two are not the same.

questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: Pop A, early in the cycle
Pop B, the trend is proven
questions.answer: Pop A, early in the cycle
questions.why: Pop A. Early in a new cycle, not the fourth base of an old one: a late-cycle base is B-. DHI popped three sessions after SPY's low in 2023.
questions.lesson_line: Early pops in a new cycle are the best ones. Late bases in old trends are tired.

wrong.Pop B, the trend is proven: A proven old trend on its fourth base is late. Late-cycle bases are B-.
wrong.They grade the same: Where the pop sits in the cycle grades it. Early beats late.

questions.story: Pop A comes three sessions after the index's own low. Pop B comes in the index's fourth month up, on the stock's fourth base.

questions.q: How does that grade?
choices: No trade, it is a chase
questions.why: B-. Overhead supply right above the pivot is a B- cue; reclaiming the 50-day too is A+. Kell's TSLA rejected at the gap resistance the day after its pop.
questions.lesson_line: Look up before you buy. Sellers waiting just overhead cap the pop.

wrong.A+, it cleared the pivot: Clearing the pivot is the trigger, not the grade. The A+ pop has clear air above it.
wrong.No trade, it is a chase: Nothing says it ran past the chase line. Overhead supply lowers the grade.

questions.story: The pop clears the pivot. Right above it sits an unfilled gap down, and the 50-day is falling just overhead.

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. A clean B-grade pop sets up. What do we do?
questions.why: Pass. Orange: only A+ setups. A B pop waits for a better market.
questions.lesson_line: The market sets how many pops I take, and which ones.

wrong.Buy full size: Full risk is for a Green market. Orange takes only A+ setups.
wrong.Buy half size: Orange is not half size for everything. It is A+ only.
wrong.Buy with a tighter stop: The stop is the day's low in every market. Orange changes what you take, not where the stop goes.

questions.q: What now?
choices: The stop stays; it is the exit
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.answer: The stop stays; it is the exit
questions.why: The stop stays. A close back under the pop day's low means the pop failed, and the stop is just under it anyway. It only moves up, never down.
questions.lesson_line: When the pop fails, the stop is already where it needs to be. Leave it.

wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down. Giving it room is how a small loss grows.
wrong.Buy more near the stop: No adding, and never to a failing pop.

questions.story: You bought a pop at 40.00, stop 39.10. Two days later it closes at 39.15, under the pop day's low and five cents over your stop.

questions.q: A $14 stock trades 1,300,000 shares a day. How many dollars a day is that, in millions?
questions.why: 18.2 million. Under the $20 million a day we need, so we pass on it.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares is the dollars. Twenty million a day or it is not on the list.

questions.q: What was it?
choices: A planned loss at a smaller size
A mistake: never buy a wide stop
A reason to widen stops next time
questions.answer: A planned loss at a smaller size
questions.why: A planned loss. By our current default, volume only grades a pop, and this one was above the base days. A stop wider than about 3% means a smaller position or a pass. You took the smaller size and the stop did its job. In our scan stops within 3% did better.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop is a reason for a small size. The loss stays small too.

wrong.A mistake: never buy a wide stop: The rule is a smaller position or a pass. A smaller position is allowed.
wrong.A reason to widen stops next time: The card says never tighten the stop to fit, and a wider stop only adds risk. The answer is a smaller size.

questions.story: A 13-day base after a 41% decline. The pop closes at the high, on 1.24x the base days' volume. The honest stop is 4.7% below your fill. You took it smaller. Day 2 takes the stop.

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: Take the loss; wait for a trigger
Buy it back at the next open
Average down, just under the stop
Widen the stop on the next one
questions.answer: Take the loss; wait for a trigger
questions.why: Take the loss and wait. A valid pop that failed; the stop did its job. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Some good pops fail. The stop keeps the cost small, and the next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Buy it back at the next open: No new trigger, no new trade. Buying back at once is revenge, not a setup.
wrong.Average down, just under the stop: No adding, and never under a stop that already said no.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next one: The stop was the rule's stop. A wider one only makes the next loss bigger.

questions.story: A 29% decline, an 11-day base, a gap open at 184.95 on 1.86x the base days' volume, closing high in its range. The next session's low takes the 182.70 stop.

questions.q: By our default rules, what happened?
questions.why: Stopped at 83.15, a planned loss. By default the stop moves to breakeven at the first trim, and it never reached 3R. AMZN did this in November 2018.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the plan. A loss at the stop is the plan working.

wrong.Stopped at breakeven, at 84.88: Our default moves the stop at the first trim. It reached 2.5R, not 3R, so the stop had not moved.
wrong.Still holding through the dip: The stop is the exit. A low of 81.50 is through 83.15.

questions.story: Bought the pop at 84.88, stop 83.15. It reaches 2.5R in two sessions, before any trim. On day 3 it trades down to 81.50.

questions.q: Bought at 60.00, stop 59.00. It gaps down; the first 30-minute low is 57.30. How many R would a stop there lose?
questions.why: 2.7R, past the 2R ceiling, so get out. On a gap through the stop the first 30-minute low is the new stop, unless that loss is past 2R.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap, the first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, I am out.

questions.q: Add to it here?
choices: No, a new trade if anything
questions.answer: No, a new trade if anything
questions.why: No adds. The full size at one price with one stop. The first pullback after the pop is the EMA Crossback, a separate setup and a new trade, not an add.
questions.lesson_line: The pop is one trade. The crossback, if it comes, is another.

wrong.Yes, add a third: Kell adds as each new range breaks. Our rule is one entry and no adding.
wrong.Yes, average up to full: The full size went on at the pop. Nothing is added on the way up.

questions.story: You hold a pop. It runs a few days, then pulls back into the rising averages and holds them.

questions.q: Weeks after the pop, the stock runs far above its averages in a climax. What do we do?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Lower the trail to hold it
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long: sell a big part into it, a judgment call. Our card calls it an Exhaustion Extension.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into the climax. The averages need time to catch up.

wrong.Add, it is strongest now: No adding, and a climax is the worst place to buy.
wrong.Lower the trail to hold it: A trail only moves up. Lowering it gives back the move.
wrong.Hold, the trail decides: The trail handles the steady part. A climax is where we sell a big part by hand.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell the 3R third at the open
questions.answer: Sell the 3R third at the open
questions.why: Sell the third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past a trim level is a gift. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for 43.00 to print: It is already past 43.00. Waiting for a lower price gives back the gift.
wrong.Sell the whole position: Only the third comes off. The rest goes on to 5R and the trail.
wrong.Only raise the stop: The trim comes first. The open past 3R is where it is taken.

questions.story: Bought at 40.00, stop 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning the stock opens at 43.60.

questions.q: Kell says to stay defensive in stocks when the index makes a Reversal Extension.
questions.why: False. Get aggressive trading individual stocks when you see a Reversal Extension on the index. Deepvue says the same: at market turning points he trades more aggressively.
questions.lesson_line: Kell watches the index first. When it shows a Reversal Extension, he gets aggressive in stocks.

questions.q: What does our card say about this one?
choices: B- at best: smaller or pass
questions.answer: B- at best: smaller or pass
questions.why: B- at best. A stop that has to be 8% or more away is B- at best; take a smaller position or skip, never tighten it to fit. CRWD in March 2021 was stopped the next session.
questions.lesson_line: A huge day can leave a huge stop. The size has to shrink to match it.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3%: Never tighten the stop to fit. A stop inside the day's range is just a guess.
wrong.A+, the volume is huge: Volume does not fix the stop. A stop 8% or more away is B- at best.

questions.story: A pop on 3 times the 50-day volume. The day's range is so wide that the stop sits 8.6% below the fill.

questions.q: Where was the buy?
questions.why: As it traded through 30.24. Buyable only as it traded through; at the close it was a chase. SLB in January 2022 started a big run from here.
questions.lesson_line: Have the alert at the pivot. The buy is the trade through, not the close.

wrong.At the close, 31.72: 31.72 is 4.9% over the pivot, past the 4% chase line.
wrong.At the next day's open: That is a guess at where it opens. Past the chase line, wait for a tight day instead.

questions.story: One wide bar runs from inside the base through the pivot, 30.24, and both averages. It closes at 31.72, 4.9% over the pivot.

questions.q: A stock is still falling hard, stretched far under its averages, on heavy volume. Is that the entry?
choices: Yes, with a stop at the low
questions.why: No. Buying the Reversal Extension low itself is bottom fishing. Kell: trading it is often best avoided; wait for the price to consolidate under the averages as it forms a tradable pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Let the low form, then let the base form. The pop is the buy, not the panic.

wrong.Yes, buy the capitulation: That is the named mistake. The pivot comes later, after a few quiet days.
wrong.Yes, with a stop at the low: There is no low yet to put it under. The pop gives a clear pivot and a tighter stop.

questions.q: Does the base still count as tight?
questions.why: Yes. A shakeout, an undercut of the prior low by 1% that still closes up in the last 3 days, also counts.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout that closes up is the base clearing out sellers. It counts.

wrong.No, the ranges must shrink: Shrinking ranges is one way in. A shakeout that closes up is the other.
wrong.No, the undercut kills it: An undercut that closes up is the shakeout our card allows.

questions.story: Inside the base, one day undercut the prior low by 1% and closed up. That was two days ago. The ranges have not shrunk.

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
questions.why: Leave it. A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up, never down when the first days are weak.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate.

wrong.Lower it to 67.00: The stop never moves down. Weak first days are what it is there for.
wrong.Cancel it and watch: Every position has a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Sell half, lower the rest: Lowering the stop on any part breaks the same rule.

questions.story: You bought a pop at 70.00, stop 68.50. Day 2 is weak and trades down to 68.70. It feels like it needs room.

questions.q: After three stop-outs on one stock this week, a fourth try is still allowed this week.
questions.why: False. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. After three, the week is done for that name.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one name. Each one is a new trade with every rule.

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.why: No. Red: mostly cash. In a Red market it is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: In a Red market the best trade is usually no trade.

wrong.Yes, full size: Full risk is for Green. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Yes, trim at 2R: A quicker trim does not change the market. Red means we stay mostly in cash.

questions.story: The market reading is Red. A clean pop sets up in a stock above its 200-day.

questions.q: Which setup is it?
questions.why: An undercut and rally. A U&R reclaims one prior low and can fire from under the averages. A wedge pop needs a tight base and a close above both averages.
questions.lesson_line: Under the averages and back over a low is a U&R. Over the averages out of a base is a pop.

wrong.A Wedge Pop: No tight base and still under both averages. A pop closes above both.
wrong.An EMA Crossback: A crossback is a dip into averages the stock already rides. This one is still under them.

questions.story: Price undercut last week's low, reclaimed it the same day and closed back above it. It is still under both averages. There was no tight base.

questions.q: Which is it?
choices: A Wedge Drop, the Pop's mirror
questions.answer: A Wedge Drop, the Pop's mirror
questions.why: A Wedge Drop. Kell's Wedge Drop is a tight range up into the averages, then a break down through them. A Wedge Pop coils under the averages and pops up through them.
questions.lesson_line: Same coil, opposite door. Where it closes tells you which.

wrong.A Wedge Pop that failed: A pop closes up through the averages. This one closed down through them.
wrong.An EMA Crossback that failed: A crossback is a pullback that holds rising averages. This one sits under falling averages and broke down.

questions.story: After a climax top and a drop, the stock coils up into its falling averages for a few tight days. Then it closes down through both of them.

questions.q: Is this a Wedge Pop?
choices: No, it never fell under them
Yes, it is on the 20-day EMA
questions.answer: No, it never fell under them
questions.why: No. A wedge pop comes from a correction that spent most of three weeks under the 20-day EMA. A base that rides above the rising averages is a breakout setup.
questions.lesson_line: Ask where the base sits. Under the averages is pop country; above them is a breakout.

wrong.Yes, it broke a pivot: Breakouts break pivots too. The pop's pivot sits under the averages after a decline.
wrong.Yes, it is on the 20-day EMA: Riding the 20-day is an uptrend. The pop comes from under it.

questions.story: A leader ran 40% in a month, then rested five weeks above its rising 20-day EMA. Today it breaks to a new high.

questions.q: Two clean pops look alike. One follows real company news; the other has none. Which grades higher?
choices: The one backed by a real catalyst
The one with no news at all
They grade the same, news or not
questions.answer: The one backed by a real catalyst
questions.why: The one with the catalyst. A catalyst behind the pop, real news or an earnings reaction after the report, is an A+ cue.
questions.lesson_line: A reason behind the move adds to the grade. The chart still comes first.

wrong.The one with no news at all: No news is not a minus, but a real catalyst is a plus on our card.
wrong.They grade the same, news or not: A catalyst is a grade cue. It lifts the pop that has one.

questions.q: What risk do you put on it?
questions.why: Sized up. A+ risks 1% to 1.5%; A and B setups trade at normal size. 2% is the absolute ceiling, and the position cap can still shrink the shares.
questions.lesson_line: Grade sets the size. A+ in a Green market is where I lean in, inside the ceiling.

wrong.0.5%, sized down: Sizing down is for B- or lower. This one is A+.
wrong.2.5%, it is A+: That is past the 2% absolute ceiling. A+ tops out at 1.5%.
wrong.0.25%, it could fail: Every pop could fail; the stop handles that. 0.25% is for B- or lower setups.

questions.story: An A+ pop in a Green market: a gap through the pivot after the index's own low, on heavy volume.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a pop. Have the ranges in this base shrunk under the averages? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; it sits above the averages
questions.why: Take it. Two weeks of shrinking bars under both averages, contraction 0.44, the tightest of our ten. The next day it popped above the pivot and both averages.
questions.lesson_line: Small bars under the averages are the coil. The pop is the release.

wrong.Pass; the base is wide: Look again: the bars get smaller into the right edge.
wrong.Pass; it sits above the averages: Price sits under its short averages here, coiling. That is where a pop comes from.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it pushes back through its averages. Did this base tighten? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; the ranges did not shrink
Take it; it is under the averages
Take it; the decline was deep
questions.answer: Pass; the ranges did not shrink
questions.why: Pass. The last 5 sessions' ranges were 1.11x the 10 before; the card wants under 0.85x. A wide, loose rebound through the averages is a remount, not a wedge pop.
questions.lesson_line: A rebound with big bars is not a coil. No tightening, no pop.

wrong.Take it; it is under the averages: Under the averages is the place. The bars still have to shrink first.
wrong.Take it; the decline was deep: A deep decline sets up a pop. It does not replace the tight base.
